_about: PRO batch 43: era 4, The Veteran (34-37), set 2.

scenarios.title: The Old Injury
scenarios.text: An old ankle injury has started affecting your preparation: it aches in the cold, it's slow on Mondays, and it's changing how you plant without you noticing.

choices.label: See a specialist
choices.result: A specialist, three states away, and a brace you hate on sight. The ankle stops changing your plant within a month, and you stop noticing the brace.

choices.label: Adjust your approach
choices.result: Your approach, adjusted around the ankle: a shorter step, a different angle. It works, and it feels like learning to kick again.

choices.label: Rest it longer each week
choices.result: More rest days, built into every single week of the season. The ankle calms down by October, and your practices get shorter, sharper and more focused.

scenarios.title: The Retirement Savings Review
scenarios.text: You go over your finances again with your advisor, but this time the question is different. Not 'how much can I spend', but 'how long does this have to last'.

choices.label: Plan for forty years
choices.result: Forty years, planned on a long spreadsheet with the advisor. It's sobering, and for the first time the numbers feel like a life, not a score.

choices.label: Bring {love_interest} in
choices.result: {love_interest} at the table, with their own questions, which are better than yours. You leave with a plan you both believe.

choices.label: Trust the plan you have
choices.result: The plan you already have, trusted for another year. Your advisor nods, mostly satisfied, and schedules a careful check-in for next spring, in pencil.

scenarios.title: The Family's Patience
scenarios.text: {love_interest} is tired of not knowing whether there'll be another season. Every spring is the same conversation, and this year they say so out loud.

choices.label: Set a date together
choices.result: A date, agreed together: after this season, you'll decide for good. The fog lifts in the house within a week.

choices.label: Explain why you're not done
choices.result: Why you're not done, explained honestly and at length. {love_interest} listens, and asks you to promise one thing: no surprises.

choices.label: Ask what they need
choices.result: What do they need from you, either way? The answer is smaller than you feared: more Sundays, and a plan written down.

scenarios.title: The Empty Nest Approaches
scenarios.text: Your kids are getting ready to leave home: college brochures on the kitchen table, a car search, arguments about which city. The house feels like it's holding its breath.

choices.label: Visit the colleges together
choices.result: A road trip to five colleges with your oldest, during the bye week. They pick the one with the best library, and you're secretly thrilled.

choices.label: Help them plan, then step back
choices.result: A plan, built together, and then you step back and let them decide. It's the hardest part of parenting so far.

choices.label: Ask {parent} how he did it
choices.result: {parent}, asked how he survived your leaving home. He laughs, then tells you he sat in your room for an hour that first night.

scenarios.title: The Younger Teammate's Question
scenarios.text: A rookie asks you, in front of everyone at lunch, whether age really matters in this league. The whole table goes quiet and waits to hear your answer.

choices.label: Tell the truth
choices.result: Yes, it matters, and here's what you do about it: sleep, recovery, honesty with the trainers. The table listens like it's a meeting.

choices.label: Make them laugh
choices.result: Only when you get up off the couch, you say. The table roars, and the rookie gets a real answer later, in private.

choices.label: Show him instead
choices.result: No answer at lunch. Instead you show him your morning routine the next day, all ninety minutes of it. He doesn't ask again.

scenarios.title: Another One Hangs It Up
scenarios.text: Another veteran from your era retires, the fourth this year. He calls to tell you before the announcement, and says you're the last one left he really talks to.

choices.label: Go to his announcement
choices.result: His announcement, attended in person, in the second row. He sees you and loses his place in the speech, and laughs about it after.

choices.label: Ask him what it's like
choices.result: What's it like, the week after? He tells you honestly: strange, quiet, a little wonderful. You think about it on the drive home.

choices.label: Plan a trip with him
choices.result: A fishing trip, planned for the offseason, with him and two other old-timers. It becomes an annual thing, and the fish are always small.

scenarios.title: One More Big Deal?
scenarios.text: Late one night you wonder whether you'll ever get another real contract, the kind with years and guarantees, or whether it's one year at a time until it isn't.

choices.label: Earn one more real deal
choices.result: One more real deal, earned the old way, starting at six the next morning. It becomes the thing you train for all summer.

choices.label: Make peace with one year at a time
choices.result: One year at a time, accepted, even enjoyed now. Every season is a gift, and you kick like you know it.

choices.label: Talk it through with your agent
choices.result: An honest conversation with your agent about the market. It's not great, and it's clear, and you sleep better knowing.

scenarios.title: The Media's Age Debate
scenarios.text: Analysts spend a whole segment questioning whether older kickers can be trusted in big moments. They show a graphic with your age on it, in red.

choices.label: Answer on the field
choices.result: No comment, and the best week of practice you've had in a year. The analysts move on to someone else by Sunday.

choices.label: Answer with a joke
choices.result: A joke at your locker about red being your favorite color. It's the clip of the week, and one of the analysts laughs on air.

choices.label: Ignore the segment
choices.result: Never watched, never mentioned. Your teammates bring it up once in the locker room, and you change the subject to lunch.

scenarios.title: The Training Load
scenarios.text: At thirty-six you have to choose, every single week: train hard and risk the body, or recover and risk the edge. The trainers have different opinions on every day of the week.

choices.label: Train hard on Mondays only
choices.result: One hard day, Mondays, and recovery the rest of the week. It's a system, and it works better than either extreme.

choices.label: Keep training hard
choices.result: Hard, every day, the way you always have. You're strong and sore, and the trainers watch you nervously from the sideline.

choices.label: Recover first
choices.result: Recovery first, training second, every week of the season. Your body feels years younger, and your leg feels a little rusty by Saturday morning.

scenarios.title: The Business Offer
scenarios.text: A former teammate offers you a role in his business after football: a gym chain, three locations, a partner's title. He wants your name now and your time later.

choices.label: Join as a partner
choices.result: A partner, with your name on the door. The gyms do well, and you spend your Tuesdays learning about payroll.

choices.label: Invest quietly
choices.result: Money, but no name and no title on anything. It's safer, and your old teammate understands, mostly, after a long lunch.

choices.label: Say not yet
choices.result: After football, you tell him, you'll talk properly. He says the offer stands, and you believe him completely, and you shake on it.

scenarios.title: The Charity Legacy
scenarios.text: You've done community work for twelve years: the camps, the hospital visits, the coat drives. You're starting to think about making it permanent, with a building and a staff.

choices.label: Start a real foundation
choices.result: A foundation, legally and properly, with a board and a director. It's a year of paperwork, and it will outlast your career.

choices.label: Partner with a charity you trust
choices.result: A charity you've worked with for years becomes your partner. They do what they do best; you bring your name and your Saturdays.

choices.label: Keep it personal
choices.result: No building, no staff, no board. You keep showing up yourself on Saturdays, which is what the kids remember anyway.

scenarios.title: The Franchise Rebuild
scenarios.text: The club starts a rebuild: younger, cheaper, faster. Veterans are expensive, and every morning there's a new empty locker. Yours has a lot of years on it.

choices.label: Be worth the money
choices.result: Worth every dollar, at every practice. If they rebuild without you, it won't be because you got slow or soft.

choices.label: Help build the new team
choices.result: The new young players, taught and welcomed by you. The coaches see you as part of the rebuild instead of a cost.

choices.label: Ask your agent to look around
choices.result: Your agent, quietly looking around the league. There's interest from a contender, and you start to wonder about a new city.

scenarios.title: The New Kicker's Contract
scenarios.text: Your likely replacement, a young kicker the club drafted last spring, signs a big contract extension. His locker is next to yours, and he looks embarrassed about it.

choices.label: Congratulate him first
choices.result: Congratulations, before anyone else, with a handshake and a joke. He relaxes, and the rest of the season is easy between you.

choices.label: Use it as fuel
choices.result: Fuel, quietly, in every single rep. You're not done yet, and the coaches notice the new edge in your practices.

choices.label: Talk to {coach} about your role
choices.result: Your role, discussed openly with {coach}. It's changing, the coach says, and they'd like you to help him grow into it.
